read.sections.0.heading.source: A building people keep working on
read.sections.0.heading.back: A building people keep caring for

read.sections.0.text.source:
A building can last for generations because people keep working on it. Roofs, walls and surfaces need different kinds of care. Some materials need regular renewal, so keeping a place does not always mean leaving every surface untouched. Conservation is care that helps valued heritage last. It means understanding what matters about a building, and how its material, use and meaning can continue.

The Great Mosque of Djenné stands in Mali, in West Africa. UNESCO names the Old Towns of Djenné as an important example of earthen architecture: building with materials made from earth. The present mosque was rebuilt in 1906–1907. That date matters. The building we see is connected with a longer religious and urban history. But its present structure should not simply be described as unchanged since medieval times.
read.sections.0.text.back:
A building lasts for many generations because people keep caring for it. Roofs, walls and surfaces need different kinds of care. Some materials must be renewed regularly. So keeping a place does not always mean leaving every surface untouched. Conservation is care that helps valuable heritage continue; it means understanding what matters in that building and how the building's materials, use and meaning can carry on.

The Great Mosque of Djenné stands in Mali in West Africa. UNESCO identifies the Old Towns of Djenné as an important example of earthen architecture, that is, building with materials made from earth. The present mosque was rebuilt in 1906 to 1907. This date matters. The building we see is connected with a longer religious and urban history, but we should not simply describe the present structure as never having changed since the Middle Ages.

read.sections.0.simpler.source:

So keeping a place does not always mean leaving it untouched. Conservation is care that helps a valued place last. It means knowing what matters about a building, and how to keep it going.

The Great Mosque of Djenné is in Mali, in West Africa. UNESCO calls Djenné's old towns a key example of earthen architecture. That means buildings made with earth. The mosque we see now was rebuilt in 1906 and 1907. The town's history is much older. We should not say it is unchanged since long ago.
read.sections.0.simpler.back:
A building lasts a long time because people keep caring for it. Roofs, walls and surfaces need different care. Some materials must be renewed often. So keeping a place does not always mean you must not touch it. Conservation is care that helps a valuable place last. It means knowing what matters in the building and how to keep it going.

The Great Mosque of Djenné is in Mali, in West Africa. UNESCO says the old towns of Djenné are an important example of earthen architecture, meaning buildings made of earth. The mosque we see now was rebuilt in 1906 and 1907. The town's history is much older than that. We should not say the mosque has never changed since long ago.

read.sections.1.text.source:
The town's wider setting explains why this mosque mattered. Djenné grew as a market centre connected with the trans-Saharan gold trade, the trade in gold across the Sahara Desert. It became important for the spread of Islam in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Waterways also linked the town with other trading places. Trade, religious learning and local building knowledge belonged to the same urban history. Islamic identity did not require copying one form of building used everywhere. People used regional materials and skills to make a place of worship suited to their setting.

Earth is a skilled building material here. UNESCO's Urban Heritage Atlas describes sun-baked earth bricks coated with mud plaster. The wooden pieces that stick out from the walls, and the shaped surfaces, give the mosque a distinctive look. The photographs in this lesson show parts of the outside in 2005. They record what was visible then; they do not show the building's condition today.
read.sections.1.text.note: UNESCO's Urban Heritage Atlas rendered แผนที่มรดกเมืองของยูเนสโก (kept as the English name only in the sources list). 'masons' as ช่างก่อ. 'trans-Saharan gold trade' as การค้าทองคำข้ามทะเลทรายซาฮารา, so the English gloss is not repeated.
read.sections.1.text.back:
The town's wider setting helps explain why this mosque matters. Djenné grew into a market centre connected with the gold trade across the Sahara Desert, and became an important town for spreading Islam in the 15th and 16th centuries CE. Waterways also connected the town with other trading places. Trade, religious learning and local building knowledge are all part of one town's history. An Islamic identity did not force people to copy one building design used everywhere; people used the region's materials and skills to build religious buildings that suited their surroundings.

Here, earth is a building material that takes skill. UNESCO's urban heritage atlas describes sun-dried earth bricks plastered with mud mortar. The pieces of wood sticking out of the walls and the shaped surfaces give the mosque its distinctive look. The photographs in this lesson show parts of the outside in 2005. They record what could be seen then but do not show the building's condition today.

read.sections.1.simpler.source:
Djenné grew as a market town. It was linked to a trade in gold across the Sahara Desert. In the 1400s and 1500s, it became important in the spread of Islam. Waterways, such as rivers, linked it to other trading towns. Trade, religious learning and building skills grew up together there. Muslims did not have to copy one style of building. People here used local materials and skills. They made a mosque that suits its place.

Earth is a skilled building material here. The bricks are made of earth and dried in the sun. Builders cover them with mud plaster. Wooden pieces stick out from the walls. The photos in this lesson were taken in 2005. They show how the mosque looked then, not how it looks today.
read.sections.1.simpler.note: 'In the 1400s and 1500s' as ในช่วงปี 1400 ถึง 1500 กว่า (keeps both numbers; KEY_TERMS gives ช่วงปี 1400 ถึง 1499 for one century). Check it reads naturally.
read.sections.1.simpler.back:
Djenné grew into a market town. The town was connected with the gold trade across the Sahara Desert. In the years 1400 to 1500-something, Djenné became an important town for spreading Islam. Waterways, such as rivers, connected the town with other trading towns. Trade, religious learning and building skill grew together here. Muslims did not have to copy one building design. People here used local materials and skills. They built a mosque that suited the place.

Here, earth is a building material that takes skill. Bricks are made from earth and dried in the sun. Builders plaster the bricks with mud mortar. Pieces of wood stick out of the walls. The photographs in this lesson were taken in 2005. They show what the mosque was like then, not today.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Care, knowledge and the people of Djenné
read.sections.2.heading.back: Care, knowledge and the people of Djenné

read.sections.2.text.source:
Looking after earthen buildings depends on knowledge and cooperation. The atlas describes Djenné's masons, the skilled builders, and how building skills are passed on. It also names the yearly plastering of the mosque as a practice that connects two kinds of heritage. Tangible heritage is the physical building. Intangible heritage is the knowledge, organisation and shared practices around it. People take part in the life of the place through work as well as worship.

Regular care does not prevent every problem. A UNESCO report from December 2009 describes extra restoration and strengthening work involving traditional masons. Restoration is work to recover or make clearer an earlier form or condition. This dated report shows that yearly surface care and specialist repairs to the structure are different kinds of work. It should not be read as a current report of an emergency still going on.

Djenné is also a town where people live, trade and learn, and want comfortable homes and public services. Conservation needs to consider those lives. Treating a place only as attractive scenery can leave out the people whose knowledge keeps it going. A careful account asks which features carry historical and cultural meaning, and how they are looked after. It also asks how decisions involve the communities who use them.
read.sections.2.text.note: 'worship' as การประกอบศาสนกิจ (standard) and การละหมาด (simpler, the everyday Muslim word for prayer). A Muslim reviewer should confirm both.
read.sections.2.text.back:
Caring for an earthen building depends on knowledge and cooperation. The urban heritage atlas describes Djenné's masons, craftsmen in building, and explains how building skills are passed on. The atlas also says the mosque's yearly replastering is a practice that joins two kinds of heritage. Tangible cultural heritage is the building itself. Intangible cultural heritage is the knowledge, organisation and shared practices around that building. People take part in the life of this place both through work and through worship.

Regular care does not prevent every problem. A UNESCO report from December 2009 describes additional restoration and strengthening work in which traditional masons took part. Restoration is work that brings back or makes clearer a past form or condition. This dated report shows that yearly surface care and expert structural repair are different kinds of work. The report should not be read as a current report of an emergency still happening.

Djenné is still a town where people live, trade and learn, and need comfortable homes and public services. Conservation must take those lives into account. Seeing a place only as beautiful scenery can make us overlook the people who use their knowledge to keep it going. A careful account asks which features have historical and cultural meaning and how those features are cared for, and also asks how decisions involve the community that uses the place.

read.sections.2.simpler.source:
Caring for earth buildings takes skill and teamwork. Djenné's masons are skilled builders. They pass their skills on to others. Every year, people put new plaster on the mosque. This links two kinds of heritage. Tangible heritage is the building itself. Intangible heritage is the knowledge and shared ways of doing things. People help the mosque through work as well as worship.

Yearly care cannot stop every problem. In December 2009, a UNESCO report told of extra repairs. Masons who use old skills did the work. Restoration is work to bring back an earlier form or condition. So the yearly plaster and big repairs are different jobs. That report is from 2009. It does not describe a problem today.

People also live, trade and learn in Djenné. They want good homes and services. Conservation must think about their lives too. A place is not just a pretty view. The people who keep it going matter. Good choices include the people who use the place.
read.sections.2.simpler.back:
Caring for an earthen building takes skill and teamwork. Djenné's masons are craftsmen in building. They pass their skills on to others. Every year, people replaster the mosque. This joins two kinds of heritage. Tangible cultural heritage is the building itself. Intangible cultural heritage is the knowledge and the ways of doing things together. People help care for the mosque both by working and by praying.

Care every year cannot stop every problem. In December 2009, a UNESCO report told of extra repairs. Masons using old skills did this work. Restoration is work that brings back a past form or condition. So the yearly plastering and the big repairs are different kinds of work. That report is from 2009; it does not tell about problems today.

People still live, trade and learn in Djenné. They need good homes and services. Conservation must think about their lives too. A place is not just a pretty view. The people who keep the place going matter too. Good decisions involve the people who use the place.

write.prompt.source: Explain why caring for the mosque needs both materials and people's knowledge. Use one detail of each from the reading.
write.prompt.back: Explain why caring for the mosque needs both materials and people's knowledge. Use one detail from the reading for each.

write.example.source: The mosque is made of earth bricks and mud plaster. This material needs care again and again, so people put new plaster on the mosque every year. People's knowledge matters too. Djenné's masons know how to do this work, and they pass their skills on to others. The building lasts because of both its earth and the people who look after it.
write.example.back: The mosque is built from earth bricks and mud mortar. This material needs care again and again, so people replaster the mosque every year. People's knowledge matters too. Djenné's masons know how to do this work and pass their skills on to others. The building lasts because of both the earth it is built from and the people who care for it.

educatorNotes.0.source: Misconception to watch for: authentic heritage must never change, or building with earth shows a lack of skill. Both hide the documented techniques and the continuing social life of Djenné.
educatorNotes.0.back: Misconceptions to watch for: that true heritage must never change, or that building with earth shows a lack of skill. Both hide the recorded techniques and Djenné's ongoing social life.

educatorNotes.1.source: Answer points for Write: earth bricks and mud plaster need suitable, regular care; masons and community practices keep the knowledge and the organised work going. Regular renewal can sustain a heritage place, while particular restoration decisions still need evidence. Simple English is fine.
educatorNotes.1.back: Answer points for the Write step: earth bricks and mud mortar need suitable, regular care; masons and community practice keep knowledge and jointly organised work going. Regular renewal helps a heritage site last, but each restoration decision still needs evidence. Simple language is fine.
